Why the tide table is wrong half the time

By Ivy Marsh

Every harbor master keeps a printed tide table on the wall, and every harbor master knows it is a little off. The table predicts the pull of the moon and the sun on a perfectly smooth ocean. Real water is never smooth, and the coast it runs into is never simple.

Wind is the biggest culprit. A steady onshore wind can pile water against a coast and raise the high tide by half a meter. Air pressure matters too. When pressure drops, the sea surface rises, roughly one centimeter for every hectopascal of drop.

The shape of the bay changes the timing. In a long narrow estuary the tide wave slows down and grows taller, so high water can arrive an hour later than the table says. Sailors learn these local habits by watching, not by reading.

Modern forecasts add live sensor readings to the old harmonic tables. They correct the prediction a few hours ahead, which is when most boats actually need to know. The printed table still hangs on the wall, though, as a good first guess and a reminder to look at the water.
